question_text: A bank designs one account for students and a different account for retirees. Which basis for segmenting is it using, and why is that basis so common?
hint: Is the bank dividing buyers by where they live, or by variables such as age and life-cycle stage?

options.option_text: Geographic, because regions and cities are easy to reach.
options.option_explanation: Geographic segmentation divides the market into units such as regions or cities. Students and retirees are defined by age and life-cycle stage, not by place.

options.option_text: Geographic, because neighborhoods share the same needs.
options.option_explanation: The bank is not dividing buyers by neighborhood. It is using age and life-cycle stage.

options.option_text: Demographic, because such variables are easier to measure.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Age and life-cycle stage are demographic variables, which are the most popular bases because they are easier to measure.

options.option_text: Demographic, because it is the only basis that is accessible.
options.option_explanation: Demographic variables are popular because they are easier to measure, not because they are the only accessible basis.

question_text: A chocolate maker builds separate campaigns for Valentine's Day and for Easter. Which behavioral variable is it using?
hint: The campaigns are organized around particular times when people buy.

options.option_explanation: Usage rate is about how much of a product people use. These campaigns are built around times of purchase.
Correct. Valentine's Day and Easter are occasions, one of the variables in behavioral segmentation.
User status groups buyers by their status as users of the product. The campaigns here follow the calendar.
Lifestyle is a psychographic characteristic, not a behavioral variable.

question_text: A segment is large and growing, but it is full of strong, aggressive competitors, and new rivals can enter it easily. Which factor makes it less attractive?
hint: Size and growth look fine. Look at the other two factors.

options.option_explanation: Correct. A segment is less attractive if it already contains many strong and aggressive competitors or if it is easy for new entrants to come in.
The segment is large and growing, so size and growth are not the problem here.
Nothing in the case is about the company's own skills or resources. The problem is competitors and easy entry.

options.option_text: A target market without shared needs
options.option_explanation: The case says nothing about buyers' needs. It describes competitors and new entrants.

question_text: A marketing team has identified a set of differentiating competitive advantages and has chosen the right ones. What is the next step?
hint: The task has three steps. Two are already done.
correct_answer_citation: Week 06 · Choosing a Differentiation and Positioning Strategy

options.option_text: Divide the market into distinct groups
options.option_explanation: Dividing the market is segmentation, which comes before differentiation and positioning.
Evaluating segments is part of market targeting, not the last step of the positioning task.
Identifying advantages is the first step, and the team has already done it.
Correct. After identifying and choosing the right competitive advantages, the third step is selecting an overall positioning strategy.

question_text: A brand offers more benefits than its rivals and charges a lower price for them. Which value proposition is this?
hint: Name the benefits first, then the price.

options.option_explanation: More for More means more benefits at a higher price. This brand charges less.
The Same for Less offers the same benefits at a lower price. This brand offers more benefits.
Correct. More benefits at a lower price is the More for Less value proposition.
More for the Same offers more benefits at the same price. This brand charges less.
